questions.stem: Which of the following is an expression for \(\int\frac{\sin^3x-\cos^3x}{\sin x-\cos x}\,dx\)?
questions.hint: Factor a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).

steps.explain: Factor the numerator as a difference of two cubes: \(a^3-b^3=(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2)\).
\(\sin x\cos x\) is \(\sin x\) times its derivative, so its integral is \(\frac12\sin^2x\).
Option B. (Equivalent form: \(x-\frac14\cos2x+c\), which is not offered.)

keyPoints.note: The numerator is a difference of cubes — factor it and cancel.

parts.stem: Explain why the domain of the function, \(f(x)=\sqrt{2-\sqrt{x}}\) is \(0\le x\le4\).
parts.hint: Both square roots need a non-negative expression inside.

steps.explain: The inner square root \(\sqrt x\) is only defined for non-negative \(x\).
The outer square root needs a non-negative expression inside it.
Both conditions must hold at the same time.

parts.answer: For \(\sqrt{x}\) to be defined we need \(x\ge0\). For the outer root we need \(2-\sqrt x\ge0\), i.e. \(\sqrt x\le2\), so \(x\le4\). Both conditions together give \(0\le x\le4\).

keyPoints.note: Need x ≥ 0 for √x and 2 − √x ≥ 0 for the outer root.

parts.stem: Show that \(f(x)\) is a decreasing function and hence find its range.
parts.hint: Show f′(x) < 0, then evaluate f at the endpoints x = 0 and x = 4.

steps.explain: For \(0 \lt x \lt 4\) both roots in the denominator are positive, so \(f'(x) \lt 0\). Hence \(f\) is decreasing on its domain.
A decreasing function takes its largest value at the left end of the domain and its smallest at the right end.

keyPoints.text: decreasing function and hence find its range
keyPoints.note: f′(x) = −1/(4√x √(2 − √x)) < 0, so the range runs from f(4) = 0 to f(0) = √2.

parts.stem: Using the substitution, \(u=2-\sqrt{x}\) or otherwise, find the area bounded by the curve and the \(x\) and \(y\) axes.
parts.hint: With u = 2 − √x: x = (2 − u)², dx = −2(2 − u) du, limits 2 → 0.

steps.explain: The curve runs from \((0,\sqrt2)\) down to \((4,0)\), so the area is
Substitute \(u=2-\sqrt x\). Then \(\sqrt x=2-u\), so \(x=(2-u)^2\) and \(dx=-2(2-u)\,du\). Change the limits too.
Rewrite the integral in \(u\) and swap the limits to remove the minus sign.

keyPoints.note: x = (2 − u)² so dx = −2(2 − u) du; the limits x = 0, 4 become u = 2, 0.

questions.hint: Let u = x⁴: then x⁸ = u² and x³ dx = ¼ du.

steps.explain: Notice \(x^8=(x^4)^2\) and \(x^3\) is (a quarter of) the derivative of \(x^4\). Let \(u=x^4\).
The \(\ln\) option would need the numerator to be the derivative of \(x^8+3\), i.e. \(8x^7\).

keyPoints.note: x⁸ = (x⁴)², and x³ is a quarter of the derivative of x⁴ — substitute u = x⁴.

questions.hint: With u = 1/x, x√(x²+2x−1) = √(1+2u−u²)/u²; then complete the square.

steps.explain: Set up the substitution and change the limits.
steps.work: \(u=\frac1x,\quad du=-\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx\ \Rightarrow\ dx=-\frac{1}{u^2}\,du;\qquad x=1\Rightarrow u=1,\quad x\to\infty\Rightarrow u\to0\)

steps.explain: Rewrite the square root in terms of \(u\) (\(u\gt 0\)).

keyPoints.note: dx = −du/u² and the limits 1 → ∞ become 1 → 0; the u² factors cancel.

questions.stem: Using the substitution \(x=\pi-u\), the definite integral \(\int_0^{\pi}x\sin x\,dx\) will simplify to:
questions.hint: After substituting, the original integral reappears on the right — move it to the left.

steps.explain: Let \(I=\int_0^\pi x\sin x\,dx\) and substitute \(x=\pi-u\), so \(dx=-du\); \(x=0\Rightarrow u=\pi\), \(x=\pi\Rightarrow u=0\).
The last integral is \(I\) again (the letter does not matter).

keyPoints.note: sin(π − u) = sin u, and the integral of u sin u is the original I again.

questions.stem: Find \(\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{4x^2-1}}\) by making a suitable substitution.
questions.hint: Let 2x = sec θ, so √(4x² − 1) = tan θ.

keyPoints.note: √(4x² − 1) suggests 2x = sec θ, since sec²θ − 1 = tan²θ.

questions.stem:
When the substitution \(x=5\sin\theta\) is used, the integral equivalent to
\(\int\frac{x^2}{(25-x^2)\sqrt{25-x^2}}\,dx\) is;
questions.hint: Replace x, dx and √(25 − x²) = 5cos θ, then cancel.

keyPoints.note: Don't forget dx = 5cos θ dθ; 25 − x² = 25cos²θ.

questions.hint: Use t = tan(x/2); the denominator becomes 9 + t².

steps.explain: Use \(t=\tan\frac x2\): \(dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}\), \(\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}\). Limits: \(x=0\Rightarrow t=0\); \(x=\frac{2\pi}{3}\Rightarrow t=\tan\frac\pi3=\sqrt3\).
Substitute and multiply top and bottom by \(1+t^2\).

keyPoints.note: t-substitution: 5(1 + t²) + 4(1 − t²) = 9 + t². Change the limits too.

questions.stem: Use the substitution \(u=x\sin x+\cos x\) to find \(\int\frac{x\,dx}{x\tan x+1}\)
questions.hint: Multiply top and bottom by cos x; du = x cos x dx.

steps.work: \(\frac{du}{dx}=x\cos x+\sin x-\sin x=x\cos x\ \Rightarrow\ du=x\cos x\,dx\)

steps.explain: Rewrite the integrand: multiply top and bottom by \(\cos x\).
steps.work: \(\frac{x}{x\tan x+1}=\frac{x}{\frac{x\sin x}{\cos x}+1}=\frac{x\cos x}{x\sin x+\cos x}\)

keyPoints.note: Write tan x = sin x/cos x and multiply through by cos x to see du/u.

questions.stem:
\(\int\frac{3x-A}{1-x^2}\,dx\) can be determined using the partial fractions \(\frac{-1}{1+x}+\frac{2}{1-x}\).

The value of \(A\) is:
questions.hint: Combine the two partial fractions into one fraction and compare numerators.

steps.explain: Put the two partial fractions over the common denominator \((1+x)(1-x)=1-x^2\).
The two fractions have the same denominator, so their numerators must be identical for every \(x\).
Quick check with \(x=0\): the original numerator gives \(-A\), and the partial fractions give \(-1+2=1\). So \(-A=1\) and \(A=-1\), which is option B.

keyPoints.note: Add the partial fractions back together; the numerator you get must equal 3x − A.

questions.hint: Split into ∫1/(4 + x²) dx and ∫x/(4 + x²) dx.

steps.explain: Split the fraction into two standard integrals.
Second integral: the numerator is half the derivative of the denominator, since \(\frac{d}{dx}(4+x^2)=2x\).

keyPoints.note: Split into an inverse-tan integral (a = 2) and a log integral (numerator = ½ × derivative of denominator).

parts.stem: If \(\frac{1}{x(\pi-2x)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{\pi-2x}\) and \(A=\frac{1}{\pi}\) find \(B\) in terms of \(\pi\).
parts.hint: Multiply through by x(π − 2x) and substitute x = π/2.

steps.explain: Substitute \(x=\frac\pi2\) to make the \(A\) term vanish.
Check by comparing coefficients of \(x\): \(-2A+B=0\), so \(B=2A=\frac2\pi\) ✓.

keyPoints.note: From 1 = A(π − 2x) + Bx, put x = π/2.

parts.hint: Integrate (1/π)(1/x + 2/(π − 2x)); note ∫2/(π − 2x) dx = −ln(π − 2x).

steps.explain: Use the partial fractions from (i), with \(A=\frac1\pi\) and \(B=\frac2\pi\).
Integrate. Watch the chain rule: \(\int\frac{2}{\pi-2x}\,dx=-\ln(\pi-2x)\). Both \(x\) and \(\pi-2x\) are positive on the interval.

keyPoints.note: Use the partial fractions from (i). Careful: ∫2/(π − 2x) dx = −ln(π − 2x).

parts.stem:
By using the substitution \(u=a+b-x\) show that:

\(\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\int_a^bf(a+b-x)\,dx.\)
parts.hint: Let u = a + b − x; then du = −dx and the limits swap.

steps.explain: Start from the right-hand side and substitute \(u=a+b-x\).
Substitute, then swap the limits to absorb the minus sign.
The letter used for the variable of integration does not matter.

parts.answer: Let \(I=\int_a^bf(a+b-x)\,dx\) and \(u=a+b-x\), so \(du=-dx\); when \(x=a\), \(u=b\) and when \(x=b\), \(u=a\). Then \(I=\int_b^af(u)(-du)=\int_a^bf(u)\,du=\int_a^bf(x)\,dx\), since the variable of integration is a dummy variable.

keyPoints.note: du = −dx and the limits a, b swap to b, a; swapping them back removes the minus sign.

parts.hint: Use (iii) with a + b = π/2: cos² becomes sin², then add the two versions of I.

steps.explain: Simplify: \(\cos\left(\frac\pi2-x\right)=\sin x\), and the denominator becomes the same as before.
Add the two forms of \(I\) and use \(\cos^2x+\sin^2x=1\).

keyPoints.note: With a + b = π/2 the integral turns cos²x into sin²x; adding gives ∫dx/(x(π − 2x)) from (ii).

questions.stem: The algebraic fraction \(\frac{x}{3(x+c)^2}\), where \(c\) is a non-zero real number, can be written in partial fraction form, where \(A\) and \(B\) are real numbers, as;
questions.hint: A repeated factor (x + c)² needs A/(x + c) + B/(x + c)².

steps.explain: The 3 is just a constant factor; take it out.
A repeated linear factor \((x+c)^2\) needs one term for each power.
Check it works: \(\frac{x}{3}=A(x+c)+B\) gives \(A=\frac13\), \(B=-\frac c3\). So option C. The \(3x+c\) options use a factor that isn't in the denominator.

keyPoints.note: The denominator has the repeated factor (x + c)²; the 3 is only a constant.

parts.hint: Substitute x = 3 and x = −2, then compare x² coefficients.

steps.explain: Coefficient of \(x^2\): the left side has none.

keyPoints.note: x = 3 gives A, x = −2 gives C, and the x² coefficient gives B.

questions.stem: Given that \(\frac{d}{dx}\bigl(x\cos^{-1}(x)\bigr)=\cos^{-1}(x)-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\), it follows that \(\int\cos^{-1}(x)\,dx\) is:
questions.hint: Rearrange the given derivative so cos⁻¹x is on its own, then integrate both sides.

steps.explain: Make \(\cos^{-1}x\) the subject of the given result.
Integrate both sides with respect to \(x\). Integrating a derivative gives back the original function.
This is option A. (Option C wrongly writes the integrand \(\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\) instead of integrating it.) Finishing the integral confirms the result:

questions.stem: Evaluate \(\int_0^{\ln2}xe^{-x}\,dx\). Give your answer in simplest form.
questions.hint: Integrate by parts with u = x and v′ = e^(−x); remember e^(−ln 2) = ½.

steps.explain: Add the two parts. The integrand is positive on \([0,\ln2]\), so a small positive answer makes sense.

keyPoints.note: Integration by parts: u = x, v′ = e^(−x). Use e^(−ln 2) = ½.

questions.stem: Let \(I_n=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}\tan^n x\,dx\) where \(n\) is an integer and \(n\ge3\).

parts.hint: Factor out tan^(n−2)x and use 1 + tan²x = sec²x.

steps.explain: Combine the two integrals and factor out \(\tan^{n-2}x\).
Since \(\frac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2x\), this is of the form \(\int f(x)^{m}f'(x)\,dx\) with \(m=n-2\).

keyPoints.note: Write the sum as ∫tan^(n−2)x (tan²x + 1) dx = ∫tan^(n−2)x sec²x dx.

parts.hint: Use I₄ = ⅓ − I₂ and I₂ = 1 − I₀ with I₀ = π/4.

steps.explain: Rearrange the result of part (i). (The same working is valid for \(n=2\), since \(\tan^0x=1\).)
\(I_0\) is just the length of the interval.
The answer is positive and small, as expected since \(0\le\tan^4x\le1\) on \(\left[0,\frac\pi4\right]\).

keyPoints.note: Use the reduction formula twice: I₄ = ⅓ − I₂, I₂ = 1 − I₀, I₀ = π/4.

questions.hint: Write sec⁴x = (1 + tan²x) sec²x and let u = tan x.

steps.explain: Split off one \(\sec^2x\), because it is the derivative of \(\tan x\).

keyPoints.note: Keep one sec²x for du and change the other to 1 + tan²x; then u = tan x.

parts.hint: Integrate by parts with u = xⁿ, v′ = e^(−x), then divide by n!.
parts.answer: By parts with \(u=x^n\), \(v'=e^{-x}\): \(\int_0^1x^ne^{-x}dx=\left[-x^ne^{-x}\right]_0^1+n\int_0^1x^{n-1}e^{-x}dx=-\frac1e+n\int_0^1x^{n-1}e^{-x}dx\). Dividing by \(n!\): \(I_n=-\frac{1}{e\,n!}+\frac{1}{(n-1)!}\int_0^1x^{n-1}e^{-x}dx=-\frac{1}{e\,n!}+I_{n-1}\). Hence \(I_{n-1}-I_n=\frac{1}{e\,n!}\), i.e. \(\frac1{n!}=e(I_{n-1}-I_n)\).

keyPoints.note: Integration by parts: u = xⁿ, v′ = e^(−x). Remember n/n! = 1/(n − 1)!.

parts.hint: Use I_n = I_{n−1} − 1/(e·n!) repeatedly, starting from I₀ = 1 − 1/e.

steps.explain: \(1-\frac{8}{3e}\) is \(I_3\) — don't stop one step early.

keyPoints.note: Find I₀ = 1 − 1/e, then subtract 1/(e·n!) four times.

parts.stem: Use integration by parts to show that \(I_n=\frac{1}{2^n}+2n\int_0^1\frac{x^2}{\left(1+x^2\right)^{n+1}}\,dx\).
parts.hint: Integration by parts with v′ = 1 and u = (1 + x²)^(−n).

keyPoints.note: Treat the integrand as 1 × (1 + x²)^(−n), with v′ = 1.

parts.hint: Write x² = (1 + x²) − 1 to turn the integral in (i) into I_n − I_{n+1}.

keyPoints.note: Split x² = (1 + x²) − 1 in the integral from (i).

parts.hint: This is I₂; use (ii) with n = 1 and I₁ = π/4.

keyPoints.note: Recognise the integral as I₂, then use the reduction formula with n = 1.

steps.explain: \(x\) is half the derivative of \(1+x^2\), and \(\frac{d}{dx}\sqrt{1+x^2}=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\).

keyPoints.note: The integrand is exactly the derivative of √(1 + x²).

parts.hint: Parts with u = x^(n−1), v′ = x/√(1 + x²); then write √(1 + x²) = (1 + x²)/√(1 + x²).

steps.explain: Integrate by parts with \(u=x^{n-1}\) and \(v'=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\), so \(v=\sqrt{1+x^2}\).
The bracket is \(\sqrt2\) (for \(n\gt1\) it is 0 at \(x=0\)). Write \(\sqrt{1+x^2}=\frac{1+x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\).

keyPoints.note: Split xⁿ = x^(n−1)·x so v′ = x/√(1 + x²) integrates to √(1 + x²).

parts.stem: By setting up a suitable inequality, prove that \(\lim_{n\to\infty}I_n=0\)
parts.hint: Show 0 ≤ I_n ≤ √2/n and squeeze.

steps.explain: The integrand is non-negative on \([0,1]\), so every \(I_n\ge0\).

parts.answer: For 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 the integrand is ≥ 0, so \(I_n\ge0\) for all n. From (ii), \(nI_n=\sqrt2-(n-1)I_{n-2}\le\sqrt2\), so \(0\le I_n\le\frac{\sqrt2}{n}\). As n → ∞, √2/n → 0, so by the squeeze theorem \(\lim_{n\to\infty}I_n=0\).

keyPoints.text: By setting up a suitable inequality
keyPoints.note: Use I_n ≥ 0 and (ii) to get I_n ≤ √2/n.

parts.stem: Use a suitable substitution to show that \(\int_0^af(x)\,dx=\int_0^af(a-x)\,dx\).
parts.hint: Let u = a − x; the limits swap and the minus sign swaps them back.
parts.answer: Let u = a − x, du = −dx; x = 0 ⇒ u = a, x = a ⇒ u = 0. Then \(\int_0^af(a-x)\,dx=\int_a^0f(u)(-du)=\int_0^af(u)\,du=\int_0^af(x)\,dx\).

keyPoints.note: Try u = a − x.

parts.hint: Use (i) with a = π/4 to turn sin 2x into cos 2x, then add the two versions of I.

Add the two expressions for \(I\): the numerators add to the denominator.

keyPoints.note: Replacing x by π/4 − x swaps sin 2x and cos 2x. Add the two integrals.
